newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks greet U.S. list of Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks greet U.S. list of Holocaust accounts.

text.p: The Swiss Bankers' Association on Wednesday welcomed the discovery in U.S. archives of a 1940s list of Jewish accounts, saying it would aid in the search for wealth that Holocaust victims may have left in Swiss vaults.

The association cautioned, however, that the list by itself was not evidence of any mistakes by Swiss banks, which have been accused by Jewish critics of withholding Holocaust accounts from legal heirs.

Independent experts in a joint committee formed by Swiss bankers and the World Jewish Congress (WJC) would have to determine whether the accounts were rightfully claimed after the Holocaust or left untouched, spokeswoman Silvia Matile said.

"We welcome any discovery of evidence that could help the work of the Committee of Eminent Persons," she told Reuters, referring to the committee of seven international experts headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Board chairman Paul Volcker.
"We want full transparency and this kind of document could help," she said.

Researchers from the WJC on Tuesday presented the names and bank records of hundreds of Holocaust victims who used Swiss banks to protect their money from the Nazis. They had discovered the list while combing through U.S. government archives.
The WJC said the list, which includes only accounts in U.S. branches of Swiss banks as of 1941, would be turned over to the Volcker commission.
"This list by itself is no evidence of any kind of improper behaviour by Swiss banks," Matile said.
"At the moment we don't know what eventually happened to the accounts, whether they were claimed by the owners, their legal representatives or heirs," she said.
Volcker's commission will meet in Zurich on Friday and may decide which international auditing firm or firms will be contracted for the actual work of examining bank records.

Swiss banks have never disputed they were a popular refuge for the wealth of European Jews fearing Nazi persecution after Hitler came to power in Germany in 1933. Many were drawn by Switzerland's strict bank secrecy and neutral status.

But the banks reject claims by the WJC that they may be sitting on billions of dollars in assets left behind by Jewish account holders murdered in the Holocaust without having passed along their secret bank details.
The banks note that a 1960s sweep for ownerless accounts left by victims of the Nazis turned up about 10 million Swiss francs, which was paid out to heirs and Jewish and refugee groups.
A renewed survey among Swiss banks late last year turned up 39 million Swiss francs in dormant accounts that may have been opened by victims of Nazi persecution.

That figure was rejected by the WJC as too low, and the Swiss Bankers' Association agreed in May to set up the Volcker commission, which is charged with making sure Swiss banks have thoroughly checked their vaults for lost Holocaust accounts.

Parliament is set to give final approval in December to a separate expert panel empowered to lift bank secrecy and conduct a sweeping review of Swiss commercial ties to the Nazis and the fate of assets placed in Switzerland before and during the war.
